The `emln` package is a valuable tool for importing, storing, and converting EMLN (Ecological Multilayer Network) data. In this section, we will demonstrate its practical application through analysis examples, including node-level analysis using an imported dataset and mesoscale analysis using a package-included dataset.

These examples will provide firsthand experience and insights into how the `emln` package can be effectively employed in real-world analyses.

# Node-level analysis with imported dataset

At this analysis level, we will compare the eigenvector centrality scores for each state node obtained using the `get_igraph` function to the centrality scores of the same nodes in a supra-adjacency matrix (SAM) using the `get_sam` function.

This comparison aims to highlight the differences between monolayer and multilayer representations. Since eigenvector centrality takes into account the entire network's influence, we anticipate no correlation. Examining the scores in different contexts offers valuable insights and alternative perspectives on node importance.

 <!-- Eigenvector centrality is a measure of a node's importance in a network based on its connections to other important nodes. -->

## Creating a Multilayer Object

Before calculating the eigenvector centrality scores for each state node, it is recommended to transform the data into a multilayer object using the `create_multilayer_network` function. This facilitates the handling of the data and ensures a smoother analysis process.

In our case, the data represents a node-aligned multiplex network consisting of three layers: trophic interactions, non-trophic positive interactions, and non-trophic negative interactions.

for detailed instructions on creating a multilayer object, please refer to the "Example with real data from Kefi 2016" section.
```{r creating a multilayer object from Kefi 2016, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Load and organize the trophic interactions matrix
chilean_TI <- read_delim('chilean_TI.txt', delim = '\t')
nodes <- chilean_TI[,2]
names(nodes) <- 'Species'
chilean_TI <- data.matrix(chilean_TI[,3:ncol(chilean_TI)])
dimnames(chilean_TI) <- list(nodes$Species,nodes$Species)

# Load and organize the negative non-trophic interactions matrix
chilean_NTIneg <- read_delim('chilean_NTIneg.txt', delim = '\t')
nodes <- chilean_NTIneg[,2]
names(nodes) <- 'Species'
chilean_NTIneg <- data.matrix(chilean_NTIneg[,3:ncol(chilean_NTIneg)])
dimnames(chilean_NTIneg) <- list(nodes$Species,nodes$Species)

# Load and organize the negative non-trophic positive matrix
chilean_NTIpos <- read_delim('chilean_NTIpos.txt', delim = '\t')
nodes <- chilean_NTIpos[,2]
names(nodes) <- 'Species'
chilean_NTIpos <- data.matrix(chilean_NTIpos[,3:ncol(chilean_NTIpos)])
dimnames(chilean_NTIpos) <- list(nodes$Species,nodes$Species)


layer_attributes <- tibble(layer_id=1:3, layer_name=c('TI','NTIneg','NTIpos'))
multilayer_kefi <- create_multilayer_network(list_of_layers = list(chilean_TI,chilean_NTIneg,chilean_NTIpos),
                                             interlayer_links = NULL,
                                             layer_attributes = layer_attributes,
                                             bipartite = F,
                                             directed = T)
```

## Eigenvector Centrality

We will now calculate the Eigenvector centrality score of each state node using the two different methods:

### Method 1: Multilayer Context

Calculating the Eigenvector centrality score of each state node using a SAM of the multilayer network.
```{r Eigenvector of SAM, echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# get the SAM
sam_multilayer <- get_sam(multilayer = multilayer_kefi, bipartite = F, directed = T, sparse = F, remove_zero_rows_cols = F)

# converting SAM to igraph object
graph_sam <- graph_from_adjacency_matrix(sam_multilayer$M,mode = "directed",weighted = NULL,diag = TRUE,add.colnames = NULL,add.rownames = NA)

# get Eigenvector scores
eigen_sam <- igraph::eigen_centrality(graph_sam, directed = T, scale = T)$vector
```

### Method 2: Monolayer Context

Calculating the Eigenvector centrality score of each state node on a per-layer basis.
```{r Eigenvector of igraph layers,echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# get a list of igraph objects as layers igraph 
g_layer <- get_igraph(multilayer_kefi, bipartite = F, directed = T)

# get Eigenvector scores of igraph layers
eigen_igraph = c()
for (layer in g_layer$layers_igraph){
  eigen_igraph <-append(eigen_igraph, igraph::eigen_centrality(layer, scale = T)$vector)
}
```

## Results

Upon comparing the eigenvector centrality scores obtained using both methods, we visualized the correlation between the two sets of scores using a scatter plot. The scatter plot was created by merging the scores into a data frame called `ec_comparison` and using the `ggplot2` package. The x-axis represented the multilayer scores from method (1), while the y-axis represented the monolayer scores from method (2).

The function `geom_abline()` adds a reference line to the scatter plot. This reference line represents a line of equality, where the x-axis values are equal to the y-axis values.
```{r plotting eigenvector comparison,echo=TRUE, eval=TRUE, include=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# merge to data frame eigenvector comparison
ec_comparison <- data.frame(eigen_sam, eigen_igraph)
colnames(ec_comparison) <- c("multilayer","monolayer")

# scatter plot using r ggplot2
ggplot(data = ec_comparison, aes(monolayer, multilayer)) + 
           geom_point(color = "blue", size = 0.75) + 
           labs(title = "Eigenvector Centrality (EC) comparison", x = "EC (monolayer)", y = "EC (multilayer)")+
  geom_abline()+
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,1))+
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1))+
  coord_fixed()
```

The deviation of the points from the reference line indicates a lack of correlation between the two sets of scores. This observation suggests that the methods used to calculate eigenvector centrality are influenced by the entire network, supporting our hypothesis. 

Our results revealed that the majority of nodes demonstrated significance within a monolayer context but lacked importance within a multilayer context. This phenomenon can be attributed to the distinct types of interactions represented by each layer in the network.

Nodes may exhibit high centrality within individual layers due to their specific roles in facilitating certain types of interactions. However, when considering the multilayer context, the importance of nodes may diminish, suggesting that their significance is specific to the types of interactions captured by each layer. This highlights the importance of considering the unique ecological processes and interactions represented by different layers when analyzing multilayer networks and interpreting node importance.


<!-- # Mesoscale level analysis with included data sets -->

<!-- At the mesoscale level of network analysis, we examine network properties on an intermediate scale that typically includes hundreds to thousands of nodes. This example demonstrates the use of `emln` to load a multilayer ecological network dataset from the emln package included data, and to detect module persistence using the popular community detection algorithm `infomap` with the `infomapecology` package. Through this analysis, we will gain insights into the temporal behavior of species communities and how they interact across multiple layers. -->

<!-- ## loading the data set using `load_emln`. -->

<!-- To begin, we need to load the data set we will be using for our analysis. the `load_emln` function loads the multilayer network data set and returns a `multilayer` object. -->

```{r loading network from datasets,  eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
data("emln68_temporal_chacoff_2020")
emln_68 <- load_emln(68)
```

<!-- ## using `infomap` with `infomapecology` to detect module persistence. -->

<!-- Once we have loaded our data set, we can start our analysis by using `infomap` with `infomapEcology` to detect module persistence. `infomapecology` is a package  designed especially for ecologist to detect modules in ecological multilayer networks. -->

```{r infomap with infomapecology, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, include=FALSE}
emln_68_to_info <- emln_68[c('extended_ids', 'nodes', 'layers')]

# rename extended_ids to intra

names(emln_68_to_info)[which(names(emln_68_to_info) == 'extended_ids')] <- 'intra'

# Set the class of d68_to_info to be the same as d68 
class(emln_68_to_info) <- class(emln_68) 

# Delete the ”layer_to" column from the "intra" dataframe 
emln_68_to_info[["intra"]] <- emln_68_to_info[["intra"]][ , -which(names(emln_68_to_info[["intra"]]) == "layer_to")]


emln_68_modularity <- run_infomap_multilayer(emln_68_to_info, relax = T, silent = TRUE, 
                                               trials = 50, seed = 497294,
                                               multilayer_relax_rate = 0.15,
                                               multilayer_relax_limit_up = 1,
                                               multilayer_relax_limit_down = 0, 
                                               temporal_network = T)

plot_multilayer_modules(emln_68_modularity, type = 'rectangle', color_modules = TRUE)+
  scale_fill_viridis_c()

# 1. Module persistence
emln_68_modules_persistence <- emln_68_modularity$modules %>%
  group_by(module) %>% 
  summarise(b=min(layer_id), d=max(layer_id), persistence=d-b+1) %>% 
  count(persistence) %>%
  mutate(percent=(n/max(emln_68_modularity$module$module))*100)

# 1.
plot_multilayer_modules(emln_68_modularity, type = 'rectangle', color_modules = T)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0,6,1))+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,40,5))+
  scale_fill_viridis_c()+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_text(size=20),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 20),
        legend.text =  element_text(size=15),
        legend.title = element_text(size=20))


# 2. Species flow through modules in time
plot_multilayer_alluvial(emln_68_modularity, module_labels = F)+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(0,6,1))+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(0,150,20))+
  labs(y='Number of species')+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_text(color='black', size = 20),
        axis.title = element_text(size=20))
```
